About TBA
Browser title:
About TBA | The Business Architect
SEO description:
Learn about TBA's business-architecture philosophy and connected approach to growth.
See the whole business. Design the next move.
The Business Architect is built around a simple idea: business decisions work better when strategy, customers, systems, people, and operations are considered together.
Business problems rarely respect org charts.
A customer experience can depend on a website, a marketing promise, a CRM record, an operational handoff, and a team with the capacity to deliver.
When those parts are designed separately, friction can accumulate between them. TBA’s approach begins by understanding the connections, then deciding where a change is likely to matter most.
This page describes the intended philosophy. Company history, team biographies, credentials, client names, and performance claims should be added only when verified and approved for publication.
Four principles that shape the work.
Start with context
Understand goals, people, constraints, and what already exists.
Connect the parts
Design across functions and systems instead of optimizing one piece in isolation.
Make it actionable
Translate analysis into priorities, owners, decisions, and a realistic path to execution.
Stay evidence-led
Use baselines, agreed measures, and feedback to evaluate change.
A blueprint for how the business works.
Not just technology architecture. A joined-up view of business goals, customer journeys, operating processes, systems, information, and the capabilities needed to grow.
Direction
Purpose, strategy, goals, priorities, and decision criteria.
Experience
Customers, propositions, digital touchpoints, and acquisition.
Execution
People, processes, systems, data, and operational feedback.

Insights
Browser title:
Insights | The Business Architect
SEO description:
Starter insights on business architecture, systems, automation, operations, marketing, and growth.
Better questions. Clearer decisions.

A practical library for people improving business systems, customer acquisition, automation, operations, and growth. These are starter editorial summaries; expand each into a researched article before publishing.
Why growth exposes disconnected systems
Growth increases handoffs, records, decisions, and customer touchpoints. Map the connections before buying another tool.
Key takeaway: Start with the customer journey and the internal processes that support it.
When should a business invest in CRM or ERP?
A useful decision begins with requirements, process maturity, data ownership, and the cost of the current approach—not a software shortlist alone.
Key takeaway: Define the decisions and workflows the system must support before comparing products.
How to identify processes worth automating
Look for repeatable work with clear inputs and outputs. Include exception handling, data quality, and human approval in the design.
Key takeaway: Prioritize by value, frequency, failure cost, feasibility, and risk.
Why more leads do not always mean more revenue
Lead quality, response time, fit, follow-up, and conversion visibility influence the journey from attention to opportunity.
Key takeaway: Trace the funnel and agree on what counts as a qualified opportunity.
Is your business ready to scale?
Readiness considers demand alongside delivery capacity, leadership bandwidth, processes, systems, and resource constraints.
Key takeaway: Test growth assumptions before committing to major expansion.
Build SOPs people can actually use
Useful procedures help people complete work consistently. They should reflect real workflows and remain easy to maintain.
Key takeaway: Document the critical path, owner, exceptions, and review date.
